Overthrown
oh-ver-THROWN
v. (past part.)
From over and throw, Saxon thrawan, to cast or hurl. Webster 1828: turned over; thrown down; ruined; defeated. In Scripture the word is used of cities, of armies, of houses in the moral sense, and of a whole generation in the wilderness.

Biblical Definition

Overthrown is what happens to what will not stand, and Scripture applies it at every scale from a household to a generation. Proverbs sets it against endurance twice: The wicked are overthrown, and are not: but the house of the righteous shall stand (Proverbs 12:7), and The house of the wicked shall be overthrown: but the tabernacle of the upright shall flourish (Proverbs 14:11). The contrast is deliberate and humbling: the wicked have a house, solid and built, while the upright have a tabernacle, a tent — and it is the tent that flourishes. Jonah’s five-word sermon uses the word as the whole message: Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown (Jonah 3:4), and the city repented, and God repented of the evil He had said He would do. Paul applies it to Israel in the desert as the standing warning to the church: But with many of them God was not well pleased: for they were overthrown in the wilderness (1 Corinthians 10:5). They had all passed through the sea, all eaten the same spiritual meat, all drunk of the Rock — and were overthrown anyway, which is why Paul adds that these things were written for our admonition.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines OVERTHROWN as turned over; thrown down or over; ruined; subverted; defeated; destroyed — applied to buildings, to armies, to governments, and to persons.

expand to see more

OVERTHROWN, pp. — Turned over; thrown down; prostrated; demolished.

Defeated; vanquished; routed, as an army in battle.

Ruined; subverted; destroyed, as a city, a state, or a design.

Applied figuratively to persons and to houses in the sense of a family or line brought to nothing.

From over and throw, Saxon thrawan, to cast — the root also of throw and overthrow.

Key Scripture

Proverbs 12:7 — "The wicked are overthrown, and are not: but the house of the righteous shall stand."

Proverbs 14:11 — "The house of the wicked shall be overthrown: but the tabernacle of the upright shall flourish."

Jonah 3:4 — "And Jonah began to enter into the city a day's journey, and he cried, and said, Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown."

1 Corinthians 10:5 — "But with many of them God was not well pleased: for they were overthrown in the wilderness."

Modern Corruption

1 Corinthians 10:5 says that men who had every covenant privilege were overthrown in the wilderness, which is the passage most directly opposed to the popular assurance that a past profession secures a man regardless of how he continues.

expand to see more

Paul’s list of what the wilderness generation possessed is deliberately sacramental: all under the cloud, all passed through the sea, all baptized unto Moses, all ate the same spiritual meat, all drank the same spiritual drink, and that Rock was Christ. Then: But with many of them God was not well pleased: for they were overthrown in the wilderness. The conclusion he draws is let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall. This is not a denial of the perseverance of the saints; the Reformed doctrine has always held that those truly regenerate will persevere and that the means of their persevering include exactly such warnings. What it denies is the popular deformation — that a decision recorded years ago settles the question and that continuance is optional. Hebrews 3 and 4 press the same generation for the same reason.

Jonah 3:4 corrects a different error, this time about prophecy. Jonah preached that Nineveh should be overthrown in forty days; Nineveh repented; God did not destroy it; and Jonah was furious precisely because he had expected this. His complaint in chapter 4 is that he knew God to be gracious… and repentest thee of the evil. A prophecy of judgment carries an implicit condition, as Jeremiah 18:7-8 states outright, and this is not a failed prediction but the ordinary way God’s threatenings work. It is worth noting to those who dismiss the prophets as unreliable, and equally to those who preach judgment without ever expecting anyone to repent of it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew haphak (H2015), to turn, to overturn — the verb used of Sodom; haras (H2040), to pull down, to break down; Greek katastronnumi (G2693), to strew down, to lay low; kataluo (G2647), to throw down.

expand to see more

Hebrew haphak (H2015) — to turn over, to overthrow; used of Sodom and Gomorrah and of Nineveh in Jonah 3:4.

Hebrew haras (H2040) — to break down, to demolish; the house of the wicked shall be overthrown (Proverbs 14:11).

Greek katastronnumi (G2693) — to strew down, to lay bodies low over a plain; the vivid verb of 1 Corinthians 10:5.

Greek kataluo (G2647) — to loosen down, to demolish; Gamaliel’s ye cannot overthrow it (Acts 5:39).

Greek anatrepo (G396) — to overturn; used of those who overthrow the faith of some (2 Timothy 2:18).

Usage

"The wicked are overthrown, and are not (Proverbs 12:7) — the built house against the standing tent."

"Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown (Jonah 3:4) — a threatening that carried its own condition."

"They were overthrown in the wilderness (1 Corinthians 10:5) — every privilege, and no perseverance."
